## Proposal Background

Microplastics are a growing concern in the world today. The amount of these microplastics has been increasing over the years and not much is known about their long term effects on living organisms. Microplastics have been observed to acquire biofilms of microscopic organisms such as bacteria and algae while in the environment (Ballesté et al., 2024).

Copepods are small, aquatic zooplankton that consume phytoplankton and are one of the most important organisms in the food chain as they consume phytoplankton and they themselves are a very abundant, protein rich food source for animals as small as fish larvae to whales. Preliminary studies have been done on marine copepods and microplastics. Studies have shown a potential hormetic curve with their CTmax when consuming a small quantity of microplastics (Zhang et al., 2025). Other studies have also pointed out that copepods are able to detect microplastics and spit them out at a success rate of up to 80% on average due to their very sensitive mouth parts. This research was done in marine copepod species, and states that they are able to reject the microplastics regardless of the presence of a biofilm (Xu et al., 2022). Other studies however, point towards varying species of copepods having varying rates of rejection of the microplastics (Fagiano et al., 2025). Also given the presence of a biofilm on a microplastic there could be some nutritional benefit to consuming it for an organism like a copepod (Botterell et al., 2020). This research project aims to find out if these microplastics covered in a biofilm have some nutritional benefit to the copepod.

## Research Questions and Hypotheses

The question being addressed is: Does aging microplastics alter how microplastics affect the physiology of a freshwater copepod?

Hypothesis

1.  Aged microplastics containing a biofilm will have some beneficial value which will keep the CTmax at typical levels.
